newsitem.title: USA: Number inflicted with E. coli poisoning rises.
newsitem.headline: Number inflicted with E. coli poisoning rises.

text.p: Ten more cases of bacterial poisoning linked to apple juice from California have been found in the western United States and British Columbia, bringing the total to 39, officials said Monday.
The Centers for Disease Control's latest count showed 19 cases in Washington state, 10 in California, four in Colorado and six in the Canadian province.
Meanwhile health officials in the state of Washington announced in Seattle that a sample of Odwalla Inc. apple juice had tested positive for the E. coli O157:H7 bacteria.
Officals warned customers not to drink any Odwalla unpasteurized apple juice, apple juice product, carrot juice or vegetable cocktail.

The Food and Drug Administration, the agency entrusted with food safety, said pasteurization of fruit juice is one option being considered to prevent future cases of a potentially fatal strain of the E. coli bacterium.
Odwalla founder and chairman Greg Steltenpohl told reporters in Denver that he was not philosophically opposed to pasteurization, but that it was too early to tell if that was the route to go.
"We think it's too early to state as to exactly what processes will change inside of our production plant regarding the production of apple juice," he said.

Arthur Whitmore, spokesman for the FDA's food safety center, said that while pasteurization would reduce risk, the process does not insure total safety because contamination can occur after the production.
Pasteurization also affects taste, Whitmore said.
Members of the fruit juice industry and FDA officials met within 12 hours after last week's announcement of the E. coli outbreak. Whitmore said the outbreak has been a "trigger" for the agency.
The company immediately recalled its products and has cooperated with federal authorities.
Young children are most susceptible to the bacterium, which causes stomach cramps followed by bloody diarrhea. In severe cases the illness can lead to kidney failure.
The cause of the suspected contamination is not yet known, but one theory is that apples that had fallen to the ground could have been contaminated with manure.
Odwalla's contracts with suppliers prohibit "windfall apples" as they are called, but Steltenpohl noted it is impossible to check every piece of fruit.
Certification of fruit suppliers is another option, and Whitmore said officials will be talking with suppliers.
Another option could be enhanced labeling of unpasteurized products, Whitmore said. Fruit juice marked "fresh" means the product has not been pasteurized.
There have been no deaths, but a 16-month-old girl remained in critical condition in Denver.
